title: CIVIL WAR Has Already Begun In Britain…
text:
by Daily Sceptic, Modernity News :
The war has already started, one broken friendship, family row and motorway blockade at a time
Professor David Betz of King’s College London has done something few academics ever manage: he has got a good part of the country talking seriously about civil war in Britain. His case is about the body politic, a fragmenting society, collapsing trust in the state, and the point at which organised groups start using violence to settle what politics no longer can.
TRUTH LIVES on at https://sgtreport.tv/
I think he’s right about the direction of travel. Where I part company with him is on the scale. Betz is thinking about organised groups and attacks on the infrastructure that keeps our cities running. I think the war has already started at the level of the individual: between brothers and sisters, between old friends, between the man in the van and the protester glued to the road in front of him. People no longer simply disagree. They regard each other as illegitimate, and in more and more everyday situations that contempt is spilling over into something physical. That, to me, is what civil war looks like before anyone hands out the guns.
The birthday party
I realised how far things had gone at a birthday party. It was for someone I’ve known since childhood, held in the basement of a bar, and the room was full of childhood friends and the people they’d collected along the way.
Even at 11 o’clock there were people wearing French berets and sunglasses. Indoors. In a basement. Perhaps that’s fashionable now, I’m prepared to accept my grasp of these things has its limits, but it set the tone for an evening among people who were very comfortable with the way they saw the world.
There were really two crowds in that room. One was the rich north London set: people who had done very well indeed and could afford their politics several times over. The other was made up of people with ordinary jobs and ordinary money worries; musicians, people who worked for Transport for London, some who’d had to move out of London to afford anything half decent. I’d be surprised if many in that second group had much in savings.
What united them was the politics. It was Ken Livingstone’s Labour, Billy Bragg’s Labour: a world where everyone knew which opinions marked you out as decent, and everyone seemed to know who the right sort of people were. I recognised it straight away, because I grew up in a version of it.
One woman summed up the mood. She worked for a green company and lobbied on environmental issues, and she had chosen to have two children without a father around – the second conceived at a fertility clinic. I asked whether the younger one ever got jealous when the older child’s father turned up, which he did now and again. She told me, more or less, that her daughter knew she didn’t need a man. It came out like a slogan. My body, my choice, I can have whatever I want, and the children will adjust.
